fragments.text: Quadratics underpin a huge share of Pure Maths 1 — from sketching parabolas to justifying whether an equation has real solutions. The key skills are solving quadratic equations by three different methods, and using the discriminant to reason about the number of roots without necessarily solving the equation.

fragments.label: Discriminant
fragments.text: The value b² − 4ac for a quadratic ax²+bx+c, which determines the number and type of roots without solving the equation.

fragments.label: Completing the square
fragments.text: Rewriting a quadratic ax²+bx+c in the form a(x+p)²+q, which directly reveals the turning point (−p, q).
Solving quadratics (three methods)

fragments.label: Solving quadratics (three methods)
fragments.text: Be fluent switching between three approaches depending on what the question wants: factorising (fastest, when it factorises nicely), the quadratic formula (always works), and completing the square (works, and reveals the turning point for free).
Completing the square & the vertex

fragments.label: Completing the square & the vertex
fragments.text: Write a(x+p)² + q. The graph's turning point is at (−p, q) — a minimum if a>0, maximum if a<0. This is the standard way to prove something is 'always positive' or find a minimum/maximum without calculus.

fragments.label: Completing the square & the vertex
fragments.text: x² + 6x + 11 = (x+3)² + 2  → minimum value 2 at x = −3
The discriminant

fragments.label: The discriminant
fragments.text: For ax²+bx+c, the discriminant b²−4ac tells you the root type without solving: greater than 0 gives two distinct real roots, equal to 0 gives one repeated root (the graph touches the x-axis), and less than 0 gives no real roots (the graph doesn't cross the x-axis).

fragments.label: The discriminant
fragments.text: x² + 4x + 4 = 0 → discriminant = 16 − 16 = 0 → one repeated root (x = −2)
Disguised quadratics

fragments.label: Disguised quadratics
fragments.text: Some equations look unfamiliar but are quadratic in disguise — e.g. in terms of x², √x, or eˣ. Substitute u for the repeated expression, solve the quadratic in u, then convert back to x.

fragments.label: Disguised quadratics
fragments.text: x⁴ − 5x² + 4 = 0 → let u = x² → u²−5u+4=0 → u=1 or u=4 → x = ±1, ±2
Discriminant >0 → 2 roots, =0 → 1 repeated root, <0 → 0 real roots
a(x+p)²+q → vertex at (−p, q)

fragments.label: Functions

fragments.label: Functions

Extend algebraic technique to harder polynomials, partial fractions with repeated or quadratic factors, and the general binomial expansion for any rational n. This guide turns the current syllabus outcomes into a connected revision sequence: learn the ideas, practise the method, then use the recall cards and checklist to diagnose what still needs work.

fragments.label: Modulus
fragments.text: |x| is the non-negative distance of x from 0.

fragments.label: Remainder theorem
fragments.text: The remainder when f(x) is divided by x − a is f(a).

fragments.label: Factor theorem
fragments.text: x − a is a factor of f(x) exactly when f(a) = 0.

fragments.label: Proper fraction
fragments.text: A rational expression whose numerator has lower degree than its denominator.

fragments.label: Binomial series
fragments.text: An expansion of (1 + x)ⁿ that is infinite when n is not a non-negative integer.
Modulus equations and inequalities

fragments.label: Modulus equations and inequalities
fragments.text: Treat |u| as a distance. For b > 0, |u| = b gives u = ±b, |u| < b gives −b < u < b, and |u| > b gives u < −b or u > b. For expressions on both sides, critical points or squaring can help, but every solution must satisfy the original relation.

fragments.label: Modulus equations and inequalities
fragments.text: Sketch y = |ax + b| by reflecting negative y-values above the x-axis.

fragments.label: Modulus equations and inequalities
fragments.text: Use interval notation or a number line to communicate inequality answers clearly.

fragments.label: Modulus equations and inequalities
fragments.text: Modulus interval: |x − a| < b ⇔ a − b < x < a + b
Polynomial division and theorems

fragments.label: Polynomial division and theorems
fragments.text: Write missing powers with zero coefficients before long division. If f(x) = (x − a)q(x) + r, then r = f(a). Use known factors to reduce a cubic or quartic, then solve the remaining factor completely.

fragments.label: Polynomial division and theorems
fragments.text: For a divisor ax + b, test x = −b/a.

fragments.label: Polynomial division and theorems
fragments.text: Match coefficients only after expanding both sides in descending powers.
Partial fractions

fragments.label: Partial fractions
fragments.text: First check that the fraction is proper. Use A/(ax+b) + B/(cx+d) for distinct linear factors, A/(ax+b) + B/(ax+b)² for a repeated factor, and (Bx+C)/(x²+d) over an irreducible quadratic. Cover-up works for simple linear factors; substitution and coefficient comparison finish the rest.

fragments.label: Partial fractions
fragments.text: Polynomial division comes before decomposition when degrees are equal or numerator degree is larger.

fragments.label: Partial fractions
fragments.text: A quadratic denominator needs a linear numerator.
General binomial expansion

fragments.label: General binomial expansion
fragments.text: Use (1 + x)ⁿ = 1 + nx + n(n−1)x²/2! + n(n−1)(n−2)x³/3! + ⋯. Rewrite expressions into this form first. The series is valid for |x| < 1, so after substituting x = g(t), solve |g(t)| < 1.

fragments.label: General binomial expansion
fragments.text: Keep exact fractional coefficients until the final line.

fragments.label: General binomial expansion
fragments.text: Only include the requested highest power; cross-terms can contribute to it.
What partial-fraction numerator belongs above an irreducible quadratic?

fragments.label: What partial-fraction numerator belongs above an irreducible quadratic?
fragments.text: Use a linear numerator, for example (Bx + C)/(x² + d).
How do you test whether x − a is a factor?

fragments.label: How do you test whether x − a is a factor?
fragments.text: Calculate f(a); it is a factor exactly when f(a) = 0.
What is the validity condition for a general binomial expansion?

fragments.label: What is the validity condition for a general binomial expansion?
fragments.text: The substituted quantity playing the role of x must have modulus less than 1.
Why check modulus solutions?

fragments.label: Why check modulus solutions?
fragments.text: Squaring or splitting cases can introduce values that do not satisfy the original equation or inequality.

Use natural logarithms and e to solve equations and model real-world growth/decay contexts. This guide turns the current syllabus outcomes into a connected revision sequence: learn the ideas, practise the method, then use the recall cards and checklist to diagnose what still needs work.

fragments.label: Natural logarithm
fragments.text: ln x is logarithm to base e and is defined only for x > 0.

fragments.label: Inverse functions
fragments.text: eˣ and ln x undo one another: ln(eˣ)=x and eˡⁿˣ=x for x>0.

fragments.label: Exponential model
fragments.text: A quantity whose rate or repeated proportional change is tied to its current value.

fragments.label: Linearisation
fragments.text: Transforming a non-linear relationship into Y = mX + c so a straight-line graph can be used.
Logarithms and exponentials

fragments.label: Logarithms and exponentials
fragments.text: Use ln(ab)=ln a+ln b, ln(a/b)=ln a−ln b and ln(aᵏ)=k ln a. A logarithm argument must be positive. The graphs y=eˣ and y=ln x are reflections in y=x; eˣ>0 for all real x, while ln x has vertical asymptote x=0.

fragments.label: Logarithms and exponentials
fragments.text: Do not split ln(a+b).

fragments.label: Logarithms and exponentials
fragments.text: When taking logs of both sides, first ensure both sides are positive.

fragments.label: Logarithms and exponentials
fragments.text: Log laws: ln(ab)=ln a+ln b; ln(a/b)=ln a−ln b; ln(aᵏ)=k ln a
Solving equations and inequalities

fragments.label: Solving equations and inequalities
fragments.text: Try writing both sides with a common base. Otherwise isolate the exponential expression and take logarithms. For inequalities, remember that eˣ and ln x are increasing, but a base a with 0<a<1 reverses the inequality when comparing exponents.

fragments.label: Solving equations and inequalities
fragments.text: Keep logarithms exact until the final numerical evaluation.

fragments.label: Solving equations and inequalities
fragments.text: Reject roots that make any log argument non-positive.
Linearising power laws

fragments.label: Linearising power laws
fragments.text: For y=Axⁿ, take logs to obtain ln y = n ln x + ln A. A plot of ln y against ln x has gradient n and intercept ln A, so A=eⁱⁿᵗᵉʳᶜᵉᵖᵗ. Units and the choice of transformed axes matter.

fragments.label: Linearising power laws
fragments.text: Gradient is the exponent, not the coefficient A.

fragments.label: Linearising power laws
fragments.text: Back-transform the intercept before reporting A.
Linearising exponential laws

fragments.label: Linearising exponential laws
fragments.text: For y=Abˣ, ln y = x ln b + ln A. A plot of ln y against x has gradient ln b. In continuous growth y=Aeᵏˣ, the gradient is k. A negative k models decay; half-life solves eᵏᵗ=1/2.

fragments.label: Linearising exponential laws
fragments.text: State the transformed variables used on each axis.

fragments.label: Linearising exponential laws
fragments.text: Interpret constants using the original model, not only the straight line.
How is y=Axⁿ linearised?

fragments.label: How is y=Axⁿ linearised?
fragments.text: Plot ln y against ln x; the gradient is n and the intercept is ln A.
What restriction applies to ln f(x)?

fragments.label: What restriction applies to ln f(x)?
fragments.text: f(x) must be strictly positive.
How do you recover A from an intercept c=ln A?

fragments.label: How do you recover A from an intercept c=ln A?
fragments.text: Use A=eᶜ.
What does k<0 mean in y=Aeᵏᵗ?

fragments.label: What does k<0 mean in y=Aeᵏᵗ?
fragments.text: The quantity decays exponentially as t increases.

Use compound and double-angle identities and the R sin(x+α) form to solve harder trig equations and find max/min values. This guide turns the current syllabus outcomes into a connected revision sequence: learn the ideas, practise the method, then use the recall cards and checklist to diagnose what still needs work.

fragments.label: Secant
fragments.text: sec θ = 1/cos θ.

fragments.label: Cosecant
fragments.text: cosec θ = 1/sin θ.

fragments.label: Cotangent
fragments.text: cot θ = cos θ/sin θ = 1/tan θ.

fragments.label: Compound angle
fragments.text: An angle written as A±B so its sine, cosine or tangent can be expanded.

fragments.label: R-form
fragments.text: A single shifted sine or cosine equal to a linear combination of sin θ and cos θ.
Reciprocal functions and identities

fragments.label: Reciprocal functions and identities
fragments.text: Know sec²θ=1+tan²θ and cosec²θ=1+cot²θ. Domain exclusions occur wherever the denominator is zero. Sketching the reciprocal graphs helps determine asymptotes, periods and all solutions.

fragments.label: Reciprocal functions and identities
fragments.text: sec and cosec have range y≤−1 or y≥1.

fragments.label: Reciprocal functions and identities
fragments.text: cot θ has period π radians.

fragments.label: Reciprocal functions and identities
fragments.text: Pythagorean identities: sec²θ=1+tan²θ; cosec²θ=1+cot²θ
Compound and double angles

fragments.label: Compound and double angles
fragments.text: Use sin(A±B)=sin A cos B±cos A sin B and cos(A±B)=cos A cos B∓sin A sin B. From these derive sin2A=2sinAcosA and the three useful forms of cos2A.

fragments.label: Compound and double angles
fragments.text: Choose cos2A=1−2sin²A or 2cos²A−1 to eliminate the unwanted function.

fragments.label: Compound and double angles
fragments.text: Preserve signs carefully in cos(A±B).
The R-form

fragments.label: The R-form
fragments.text: For a sinθ+b cosθ=R sin(θ+α), compare coefficients: Rcosα=a and Rsinα=b, so R=√(a²+b²). The interval/quadrant for α must match both signs. The form makes extrema and equations easier.

fragments.label: The R-form
fragments.text: Maximum is R and minimum is −R before any vertical shift.

fragments.label: The R-form
fragments.text: Use a sketch to decide which inverse-trig solution is appropriate.
Solving trigonometric equations

fragments.label: Solving trigonometric equations
fragments.text: Reduce to one trig function or R-form, solve the basic equation, then generate every solution in the requested interval. Work in radians unless degrees are stated. Check any values lost by dividing by sinθ or cosθ.

fragments.label: Solving trigonometric equations
fragments.text: Write the general symmetry pattern before filtering the interval.

fragments.label: Solving trigonometric equations
fragments.text: Do not cancel a trig factor unless its zero case has been considered.
How do you find R in a sinθ+b cosθ?

fragments.label: How do you find R in a sinθ+b cosθ?
fragments.text: R=√(a²+b²).
Which identity converts 1+tan²θ?

fragments.label: Which identity converts 1+tan²θ?
fragments.text: 1+tan²θ=sec²θ.
Why must divided trig factors be checked separately?

fragments.label: Why must divided trig factors be checked separately?
fragments.text: A factor may be zero, and dividing by it would discard valid solutions.
What is the range of R sin(θ+α)+c?

fragments.label: What is the range of R sin(θ+α)+c?
fragments.text: From c−R to c+R inclusive.

Differentiate implicitly and parametrically, on top of product/quotient/chain rules, for curves not given simply as y = f(x). This guide turns the current syllabus outcomes into a connected revision sequence: learn the ideas, practise the method, then use the recall cards and checklist to diagnose what still needs work.

fragments.label: Implicit relation
fragments.text: An equation connecting x and y without y isolated as a function of x.

fragments.label: Parametric equations
fragments.text: Equations x=f(t), y=g(t) describing a curve through a parameter t.

fragments.label: Stationary point
fragments.text: A point where dy/dx=0.

fragments.label: Normal
fragments.text: A line perpendicular to the tangent at the point of contact.

fragments.label: Chain rule
fragments.text: A rule for differentiating a composite function by multiplying derivatives through its layers.
Core derivatives and chain rule

fragments.label: Core derivatives and chain rule
fragments.text: Memorise d(eˣ)/dx=eˣ, d(ln x)/dx=1/x, d(sin x)/dx=cos x, d(cos x)/dx=−sin x, d(tan x)/dx=sec²x and d(tan⁻¹x)/dx=1/(1+x²). For f(g(x)), multiply f′(g(x)) by g′(x).

fragments.label: Core derivatives and chain rule
fragments.text: Trig derivative formulae assume radians.

fragments.label: Core derivatives and chain rule
fragments.text: ln|u| differentiates to u′/u wherever u≠0.

fragments.label: Core derivatives and chain rule
fragments.text: Product rule: d(uv)/dx=u(dv/dx)+v(du/dx)
Products and quotients

fragments.label: Products and quotients
fragments.text: For y=uv, y′=u′v+uv′. For y=u/v, y′=(vu′−uv′)/v². Label u and v first and simplify after differentiating, especially when a second derivative is required.

fragments.label: Products and quotients
fragments.text: The quotient-rule numerator order is denominator×derivative of numerator minus numerator×derivative of denominator.

fragments.label: Products and quotients
fragments.text: A product can sometimes be rewritten to use the chain rule more cleanly.
Implicit differentiation

fragments.label: Implicit differentiation
fragments.text: Differentiate every term with respect to x and attach dy/dx whenever a y-term is differentiated. Collect all dy/dx terms on one side and factor. Substitute the point only after obtaining a usable derivative expression.

fragments.label: Implicit differentiation
fragments.text: d(y²)/dx=2y(dy/dx).

fragments.label: Implicit differentiation
fragments.text: For xy use the product rule: d(xy)/dx=y+x(dy/dx).
Parametric differentiation

fragments.label: Parametric differentiation
fragments.text: If x=f(t) and y=g(t), then dy/dx=(dy/dt)/(dx/dt), provided dx/dt≠0. For d²y/dx², differentiate dy/dx with respect to t and divide by dx/dt again.

fragments.label: Parametric differentiation
fragments.text: Find the parameter value corresponding to the stated point.

fragments.label: Parametric differentiation
fragments.text: Normal gradient is −1/(dy/dx) when the tangent gradient is non-zero.
How is dy/dx found from x=f(t), y=g(t)?

fragments.label: How is dy/dx found from x=f(t), y=g(t)?
fragments.text: Divide dy/dt by dx/dt.
What happens when y² is differentiated implicitly?

fragments.label: What happens when y² is differentiated implicitly?
fragments.text: It becomes 2y(dy/dx).
What is the normal gradient?

fragments.label: What is the normal gradient?
fragments.text: It is the negative reciprocal of the tangent gradient, when defined.
Why are radians essential for trig differentiation?

fragments.label: Why are radians essential for trig differentiation?
fragments.text: The standard derivative formulae for sin x, cos x and tan x are valid without extra factors only in radians.

Use integration by parts, substitution and partial fractions to integrate a wider range of functions, including trig integrals. This guide turns the current syllabus outcomes into a connected revision sequence: learn the ideas, practise the method, then use the recall cards and checklist to diagnose what still needs work.

fragments.label: Substitution
fragments.text: Replacing an expression by a new variable to simplify an integral.

fragments.label: Integration by parts
fragments.text: A product-rule rearrangement used to integrate products.

fragments.label: Definite integral
fragments.text: A signed accumulated quantity evaluated between fixed limits.

fragments.label: Partial fractions
fragments.text: A decomposition that turns a rational expression into simpler integrable terms.

fragments.label: Constant of integration
fragments.text: The arbitrary constant required for an indefinite integral.
Standard reverse derivatives

fragments.label: Standard reverse derivatives
fragments.text: Recognise ∫f′(x)/f(x) dx=ln|f(x)|+C and ∫eᵃˣ⁺ᵇ dx=eᵃˣ⁺ᵇ/a+C. Similarly account for the inner derivative in sin(ax+b), cos(ax+b) and sec²(ax+b).

fragments.label: Standard reverse derivatives
fragments.text: Use ln|f(x)| unless the domain guarantees f(x)>0.

fragments.label: Standard reverse derivatives
fragments.text: Differentiate the result mentally to check the scale factor.

fragments.label: Standard reverse derivatives
fragments.text: Integration by parts: ∫u(dv/dx)dx=uv−∫v(du/dx)dx
Substitution

fragments.label: Substitution
fragments.text: Choose u for the repeated inner expression, calculate du, and rewrite every x and dx term. For definite integrals either change both limits to u-values or return fully to x before applying the original limits.

fragments.label: Substitution
fragments.text: A substitution is incomplete if x remains in the new integrand.

fragments.label: Substitution
fragments.text: Write new bounds beside u=… to avoid mixing variables.
Integration by parts

fragments.label: Integration by parts
fragments.text: Use ∫u(dv/dx)dx=uv−∫v(du/dx)dx. Choose u so it becomes simpler when differentiated—commonly logarithmic or algebraic before trig/exponential. Repeated use may be needed.

fragments.label: Integration by parts
fragments.text: For ∫ln x dx, take dv/dx=1.

fragments.label: Integration by parts
fragments.text: Keep brackets around the second integral to protect the minus sign.
Partial fractions and trig identities

fragments.label: Partial fractions and trig identities
fragments.text: Decompose rational functions before integrating; repeated linear terms lead to powers such as (ax+b)⁻². For sin²x or cos²x use double-angle identities. Some integrals need a sequence: algebraic division, partial fractions, then standard forms.

fragments.label: Partial fractions and trig identities
fragments.text: A 1/(x²+a²) term integrates to an arctangent form.

fragments.label: Partial fractions and trig identities
fragments.text: Simplify the integrand before choosing a method.
When should limits be changed in substitution?

fragments.label: When should limits be changed in substitution?
fragments.text: When the integral is rewritten in the new variable; otherwise return completely to x before using x-limits.
What is a strong choice for u in ∫x eˣ dx?

fragments.label: What is a strong choice for u in ∫x eˣ dx?
fragments.text: Choose u=x because differentiation simplifies it, and integrate eˣ as dv/dx.
Which pattern gives a logarithm?

fragments.label: Which pattern gives a logarithm?
fragments.text: An integrand of the form f′(x)/f(x).
How can ∫cos²x dx be made integrable?

fragments.label: How can ∫cos²x dx be made integrable?
fragments.text: Use cos²x=(1+cos2x)/2.

Apply iterative methods to harder equations, justifying convergence and the accuracy of your final answer. This guide turns the current syllabus outcomes into a connected revision sequence: learn the ideas, practise the method, then use the recall cards and checklist to diagnose what still needs work.

fragments.label: Root
fragments.text: A value α for which f(α)=0.

fragments.label: Iteration
fragments.text: Repeatedly applying xₙ₊₁=F(xₙ) to generate approximations.

fragments.label: Convergence
fragments.text: The approximations approach a fixed limiting value.

fragments.label: Sign change
fragments.text: f(a) and f(b) have opposite signs, guaranteeing at least one root in (a,b) when f is continuous.

fragments.label: Fixed point
fragments.text: A value α satisfying α=F(α).
Locating a root

fragments.label: Locating a root
fragments.text: For continuous f, calculate f(a) and f(b). If f(a)f(b)<0, at least one root lies between a and b. A graph helps choose a sensible interval, but a sign change alone does not prove uniqueness.

fragments.label: Locating a root
fragments.text: State continuity when giving a formal sign-change justification.

fragments.label: Locating a root
fragments.text: An even-multiplicity root may touch the axis without changing sign.

fragments.label: Locating a root
fragments.text: Sign-change test: f(a)f(b)<0 ⇒ at least one root in (a,b), if f is continuous
Building an iteration

fragments.label: Building an iteration
fragments.text: Rearrange f(x)=0 into x=F(x), then use xₙ₊₁=F(xₙ). Different rearrangements can converge, oscillate or diverge. Use the starting value given and retain calculator precision through the table.

fragments.label: Building an iteration
fragments.text: Show enough consecutive values for the examiner to follow the process.

fragments.label: Building an iteration
fragments.text: Do not replace F(xₙ) with f(xₙ).
Understanding convergence

fragments.label: Understanding convergence
fragments.text: A convergent sequence settles near a fixed point α where α=F(α). Cobweb thinking explains why some iterations move toward the intersection y=F(x), y=x and others move away; the syllabus expects recognition of failure even if the derivative test is not required.

fragments.label: Understanding convergence
fragments.text: Oscillation may still converge if its size shrinks.

fragments.label: Understanding convergence
fragments.text: A calculator error message can indicate the rearrangement leaves its valid domain.
Proving the stated accuracy

fragments.label: Proving the stated accuracy
fragments.text: A rounded decimal needs a bracket around the true root. For a value r correct to k decimal places, test the half-unit boundaries r±0.5×10⁻ᵏ and show f changes sign there, assuming continuity and a single relevant root.

fragments.label: Proving the stated accuracy
fragments.text: Repeated equal displayed iterates suggest accuracy but do not by themselves prove it.

fragments.label: Proving the stated accuracy
fragments.text: Use unrounded boundaries and function values.
What must accompany a sign change to guarantee a root?

fragments.label: What must accompany a sign change to guarantee a root?
fragments.text: Continuity of f on the interval.
What equation does the limit of xₙ₊₁=F(xₙ) satisfy?

fragments.label: What equation does the limit of xₙ₊₁=F(xₙ) satisfy?
fragments.text: The fixed-point equation α=F(α).
How do you justify a root to 3 decimal places?

fragments.label: How do you justify a root to 3 decimal places?
fragments.text: Show a sign change at the two rounding boundaries r±0.0005, with the relevant continuity/uniqueness context.
Can a root exist without a sign change?

fragments.label: Can a root exist without a sign change?
fragments.text: Yes; an even-multiplicity root can touch the axis and turn back.

Revise 3D lines, dot product, angles/intersections. This guide turns the current syllabus outcomes into a connected revision sequence: learn the ideas, practise the method, then use the recall cards and checklist to diagnose what still needs work.

fragments.label: Position vector
fragments.text: The vector from the origin to a point.

fragments.label: Direction vector
fragments.text: Any non-zero vector parallel to a line.

fragments.label: Unit vector
fragments.text: A vector of magnitude 1.

fragments.label: Scalar product
fragments.text: a·b=|a||b|cosθ, producing a scalar.

fragments.label: Skew lines
fragments.text: Non-parallel lines in 3D that do not intersect.
Vector operations

fragments.label: Vector operations
fragments.text: For a=(a₁,a₂,a₃), |a|=√(a₁²+a₂²+a₃²) and the unit vector in its direction is a/|a|. If A and B have position vectors a and b, then AB=b−a and the midpoint is (a+b)/2.

fragments.label: Vector operations
fragments.text: A displacement vector has direction; distance is its magnitude.

fragments.label: Vector operations
fragments.text: Use exact radicals unless a decimal is requested.

fragments.label: Vector operations
fragments.text: Magnitude: |a|=√(a₁²+a₂²+a₃²)
Vector equations of lines

fragments.label: Vector equations of lines
fragments.text: The line through point A with position vector a and direction b is r=a+λb. Through A and B, use direction b−a. Direction vectors can be scalar multiples and still describe parallel lines.

fragments.label: Vector equations of lines
fragments.text: The parameter is a scalar, not a vector component.

fragments.label: Vector equations of lines
fragments.text: Read a point from the fixed vector and direction from the coefficient of λ.
Intersections and skew lines

fragments.label: Intersections and skew lines
fragments.text: Equate the x, y and z components of two line equations. Solve two equations for the two parameters, then test the third. If it fails, non-parallel lines are skew; if directions are multiples, test whether a point lies on both lines.

fragments.label: Intersections and skew lines
fragments.text: Always perform the third-component check.

fragments.label: Intersections and skew lines
fragments.text: Report the point of intersection, not only parameter values.
Scalar products and perpendicularity

fragments.label: Scalar products and perpendicularity
fragments.text: Compute a·b=a₁b₁+a₂b₂+a₃b₃. Perpendicular vectors have dot product 0. For an angle use cosθ=(a·b)/(|a||b|); for the acute angle between lines, reverse a direction if necessary or use |a·b|.

fragments.label: Scalar products and perpendicularity
fragments.text: A foot of a perpendicular lies on the line and its displacement to the external point has zero dot product with the line direction.

fragments.label: Scalar products and perpendicularity
fragments.text: Shortest distance between skew lines is outside this syllabus.
How do you form AB from position vectors?

fragments.label: How do you form AB from position vectors?
fragments.text: AB=OB−OA.
How do you distinguish intersecting and skew lines?

fragments.label: How do you distinguish intersecting and skew lines?
fragments.text: Solve two component equations for the parameters and check the third; failure for non-parallel lines means skew.
What does a·b=0 show?

fragments.label: What does a·b=0 show?
fragments.text: The non-zero vectors are perpendicular.
How is the foot from P to r=a+λb found?

fragments.label: How is the foot from P to r=a+λb found?
fragments.text: Let Q=a+λb and solve (P−Q)·b=0 for λ.

Form and solve first-order differential equations by separating variables, using given initial conditions to find a particular solution. This guide turns the current syllabus outcomes into a connected revision sequence: learn the ideas, practise the method, then use the recall cards and checklist to diagnose what still needs work.

fragments.label: Differential equation
fragments.text: An equation involving a function and one or more of its derivatives.

fragments.label: Separable
fragments.text: A first-order equation that can be rearranged with all y terms with dy and all x terms with dx.

fragments.label: General solution
fragments.text: A family of solutions containing an arbitrary constant.

fragments.label: Initial condition
fragments.text: A known value such as y=y₀ when x=x₀ that selects one solution.

fragments.label: Constant of proportionality
fragments.text: A constant k introduced when a rate is said to be proportional to a quantity.
Forming the model

fragments.label: Forming the model
fragments.text: Translate phrases literally: 'rate of increase of y is proportional to y' gives dy/dt=ky; 'rate is proportional to the remaining amount' gives dM/dt=k(M₀−M). Choose the sign from whether the quantity increases or decreases.

fragments.label: Forming the model
fragments.text: Define variables and units before forming the equation.

fragments.label: Forming the model
fragments.text: A constant of proportionality is not automatically positive if its sign is already built into the model.

fragments.label: Forming the model
fragments.text: Separation pattern: dy/dx=g(x)h(y) ⇒ ∫[1/h(y)]dy=∫g(x)dx
Separating variables

fragments.label: Separating variables
fragments.text: From dy/dx=g(x)h(y), rearrange dy/h(y)=g(x)dx and integrate both sides. Separation must happen before integration. Use logarithmic absolute values where needed.

fragments.label: Separating variables
fragments.text: Never move dy/dx as though dy and dx were ordinary numbers without showing a valid separated form.

fragments.label: Separating variables
fragments.text: Check that dividing by h(y) has not discarded an equilibrium solution h(y)=0.
Applying initial conditions

fragments.label: Applying initial conditions
fragments.text: After integrating, include a constant and substitute the condition. Sometimes exponentiating produces a multiplicative constant more naturally. Leave an implicit solution if the question allows it; otherwise isolate y.

fragments.label: Applying initial conditions
fragments.text: Apply the condition to the integrated equation, not the original derivative.

fragments.label: Applying initial conditions
fragments.text: Use exact constants until the final numerical answer.
Interpreting and checking

fragments.label: Interpreting and checking
fragments.text: Differentiate the proposed solution to check it satisfies the differential equation and initial condition. In context, reject impossible branches and describe long-term behaviour, limiting values, monotonicity or the meaning of k.

fragments.label: Interpreting and checking
fragments.text: A mathematical solution may violate physical restrictions such as mass≥0.

fragments.label: Interpreting and checking
fragments.text: State units for time constants and rates.
What comes before integrating a separable equation?

fragments.label: What comes before integrating a separable equation?
fragments.text: Rearrange so all y terms accompany dy and all x terms accompany dx.
What does an initial condition do?

fragments.label: What does an initial condition do?
fragments.text: It determines the arbitrary constant and selects a particular solution.
What solution can be lost by dividing by h(y)?

fragments.label: What solution can be lost by dividing by h(y)?
fragments.text: Any constant equilibrium solution satisfying h(y)=0.
How do you check a differential-equation solution?

fragments.label: How do you check a differential-equation solution?
fragments.text: Differentiate it and substitute into both the equation and the initial condition.

Revise Argand diagrams, modulus/argument, polar form. This guide turns the current syllabus outcomes into a connected revision sequence: learn the ideas, practise the method, then use the recall cards and checklist to diagnose what still needs work.

fragments.label: Complex number
fragments.text: z=x+iy, where i²=−1 and x,y are real.

fragments.label: Conjugate
fragments.text: For z=x+iy, z*=x−iy.

fragments.label: Modulus
fragments.text: |z|=√(x²+y²), the distance from the origin.

fragments.label: Argument
fragments.text: arg z is the directed angle from the positive real axis to z.

fragments.label: Argand diagram
fragments.text: A plane with real part horizontally and imaginary part vertically.
Cartesian arithmetic

fragments.label: Cartesian arithmetic
fragments.text: Add real and imaginary parts separately and use i²=−1 when multiplying. To divide by c+id, multiply numerator and denominator by c−id so the denominator becomes c²+d². Equality requires both real parts and imaginary parts to match.

fragments.label: Cartesian arithmetic
fragments.text: z z*=|z|².

fragments.label: Cartesian arithmetic
fragments.text: Real-coefficient polynomial roots occur in conjugate pairs.

fragments.label: Cartesian arithmetic
fragments.text: Modulus: |x+iy|=√(x²+y²)
Polar form

fragments.label: Polar form
fragments.text: Write z=r(cosθ+i sinθ), where r=|z| and θ=arg z. On multiplication, multiply moduli and add arguments; on division, divide moduli and subtract arguments. Give the argument in the interval requested.

fragments.label: Polar form
fragments.text: Use atan2 thinking or a sketch to choose the correct quadrant.

fragments.label: Polar form
fragments.text: The principal argument is commonly −π<θ≤π.
Square roots and equations

fragments.label: Square roots and equations
fragments.text: For w²=z, let w=a+ib and compare real and imaginary parts, using a²+b²=|z| as a second relation. The two roots are opposites. For polynomial questions, include the conjugate of any given non-real root, form the quadratic factor and divide.

fragments.label: Square roots and equations
fragments.text: Show exact Cartesian working for square roots.

fragments.label: Square roots and equations
fragments.text: Check by squaring the final roots.
Loci

fragments.label: Loci
fragments.text: |z−a|=r is a circle centred at a; |z−a|<r is its interior. |z−a|=|z−b| is the perpendicular bisector of AB. arg(z−a)=α is a ray from a, with the initial point excluded.

fragments.label: Loci
fragments.text: Use solid or dashed boundaries to distinguish inclusive and strict inequalities.

fragments.label: Loci
fragments.text: Shade only after testing a simple point.
Why multiply by a conjugate when dividing?

fragments.label: Why multiply by a conjugate when dividing?
fragments.text: It makes the denominator real because (c+id)(c−id)=c²+d².
What locus is |z−a|=r?

fragments.label: What locus is |z−a|=r?
fragments.text: A circle centred at a with radius r.
What happens to arguments when complex numbers are divided?

fragments.label: What happens to arguments when complex numbers are divided?
fragments.text: Subtract the divisor's argument from the numerator's argument.
If a real polynomial has root 2+3i, what else is a root?

fragments.label: If a real polynomial has root 2+3i, what else is a root?
fragments.text: 2−3i, its conjugate.

Draw force diagrams, resolve forces into components, and apply equilibrium conditions including friction. This guide turns the current syllabus outcomes into a connected revision sequence: learn the ideas, practise the method, then use the recall cards and checklist to diagnose what still needs work.

fragments.label: Equilibrium
fragments.text: A state with zero resultant force, so acceleration is zero.

fragments.label: Normal reaction
fragments.text: The contact force perpendicular to a surface.

fragments.label: Friction
fragments.text: A contact force opposing actual or impending relative motion.

fragments.label: Limiting equilibrium
fragments.text: The state just before slipping, when friction reaches μR.

fragments.label: Particle model
fragments.text: An object treated as having mass but negligible size and rotation.
Building the force diagram

fragments.label: Building the force diagram
fragments.text: Isolate one particle and draw every external force: weight mg vertically down, normal reaction perpendicular to contact, tension along a string and friction along a rough surface. Never draw motion or acceleration as a force.

fragments.label: Building the force diagram
fragments.text: Choose axes parallel and perpendicular to an incline.

fragments.label: Building the force diagram
fragments.text: Label each force once with a clear direction.

fragments.label: Building the force diagram
fragments.text: Weight: W=mg
Resolving and equilibrium

fragments.label: Resolving and equilibrium
fragments.text: For equilibrium, the vector sum of forces is zero. Resolve independently in two perpendicular directions. On an incline of angle θ, weight components are mg sinθ down the plane and mg cosθ into the plane.

fragments.label: Resolving and equilibrium
fragments.text: Equilibrium does not mean no forces; it means they balance.

fragments.label: Resolving and equilibrium
fragments.text: Use exact trig values until the end.
Friction

fragments.label: Friction
fragments.text: Friction adjusts up to a maximum μR. Use F=μR only when the particle is on the point of slipping or in limiting equilibrium. Decide its direction by imagining how the particle would move without friction.

fragments.label: Friction
fragments.text: In non-limiting equilibrium, F may be less than μR.

fragments.label: Friction
fragments.text: The normal reaction is not always mg.
Connected or angled forces

fragments.label: Connected or angled forces
fragments.text: When a string or applied force is angled, resolve it before writing equations. A vertical component can change R and therefore the maximum friction. Check that any calculated friction satisfies F≤μR.

fragments.label: Connected or angled forces
fragments.text: A pull with an upward component reduces R.

fragments.label: Connected or angled forces
fragments.text: State whether the model is smooth or rough.
When may F=μR be used?

fragments.label: When may F=μR be used?
fragments.text: Only at limiting equilibrium or when the question states the friction is limiting.
Which way does friction act?

fragments.label: Which way does friction act?
fragments.text: Opposite actual or impending relative motion between the surfaces.
What does equilibrium imply about resultant force?

fragments.label: What does equilibrium imply about resultant force?
fragments.text: The resultant is zero in every direction.
Why can R differ from mg?

fragments.label: Why can R differ from mg?
fragments.text: Other forces may have perpendicular or vertical components, and an incline changes the resolution.

title: Kinematics of motion in a straight line

fragments.text: Use SUVAT equations, motion graphs and calculus to describe motion in a straight line, including under gravity. This guide turns the current syllabus outcomes into a connected revision sequence: learn the ideas, practise the method, then use the recall cards and checklist to diagnose what still needs work.

fragments.label: Displacement
fragments.text: Signed change of position from a reference point.

fragments.label: Velocity
fragments.text: Rate of change of displacement.

fragments.label: Acceleration
fragments.text: Rate of change of velocity.

fragments.label: Speed
fragments.text: Magnitude of velocity.

fragments.label: Constant acceleration
fragments.text: Motion for which acceleration has a fixed value over the interval.
Signs and variables

fragments.label: Signs and variables
fragments.text: Choose one positive direction and keep it throughout. Displacement and velocity can be negative; speed and distance cannot. Turning points occur when v=0 and the sign of v changes.

fragments.label: Signs and variables
fragments.text: State the positive direction in vertical-motion work.

fragments.label: Signs and variables
fragments.text: A negative acceleration does not always mean slowing down.

fragments.label: Signs and variables
fragments.text: Calculus: v=ds/dt; a=dv/dt=v·dv/ds
Motion graphs

fragments.label: Motion graphs
fragments.text: Gradient of an s–t graph is velocity; gradient of a v–t graph is acceleration; signed area under v–t is displacement. Total distance requires adding the magnitudes of areas or splitting where v changes sign.

fragments.label: Motion graphs
fragments.text: Horizontal v–t segments mean constant velocity.

fragments.label: Motion graphs
fragments.text: An area below the time axis contributes negative displacement.
Calculus links

fragments.label: Calculus links
fragments.text: Use v=ds/dt and a=dv/dt=v(dv/ds). Integrate acceleration to find velocity and integrate velocity to find displacement, applying initial conditions after each integration.

fragments.label: Calculus links
fragments.text: The v dv/ds form is useful when time is absent.

fragments.label: Calculus links
fragments.text: Include constants of integration.
SUVAT and gravity

fragments.label: SUVAT and gravity
fragments.text: Use v=u+at, s=ut+½at², v²=u²+2as, and s=(u+v)t/2 only on an interval of constant acceleration. For free vertical motion take acceleration as ±g according to the chosen positive direction.

fragments.label: SUVAT and gravity
fragments.text: At maximum height v=0, not a=0.

fragments.label: SUVAT and gravity
fragments.text: Use g=10 m s⁻² in this component unless told otherwise.
What is the area under a velocity–time graph?

fragments.label: What is the area under a velocity–time graph?
fragments.text: Signed displacement.
How is total distance found when velocity changes sign?

fragments.label: How is total distance found when velocity changes sign?
fragments.text: Split at v=0 and add the magnitudes of the displacements.
What is acceleration at maximum height?

fragments.label: What is acceleration at maximum height?
fragments.text: It is still g downward; only velocity is zero.
When are SUVAT formulae valid?

fragments.label: When are SUVAT formulae valid?
fragments.text: Only while acceleration is constant over the interval considered.

Apply conservation of momentum and impulse to collisions between particles. This guide turns the current syllabus outcomes into a connected revision sequence: learn the ideas, practise the method, then use the recall cards and checklist to diagnose what still needs work.

fragments.label: Linear momentum
fragments.text: Mass multiplied by velocity; its direction follows the velocity.

fragments.label: Direct impact
fragments.text: A collision in which motion is along one straight line.

fragments.label: Conservation of momentum
fragments.text: Total momentum is unchanged when external impulse during the interaction is negligible.

fragments.label: Coalescence
fragments.text: Bodies join and move with a common velocity after impact.

fragments.label: System
fragments.text: The collection of bodies chosen for a conservation equation.
Momentum as a vector

fragments.label: Momentum as a vector
fragments.text: Choose a positive direction and write each momentum as mv with a signed velocity. Momentum has units kg m s⁻¹. A negative result means motion opposite to the chosen direction, not negative speed.

fragments.label: Momentum as a vector
fragments.text: Mass is always positive.

fragments.label: Momentum as a vector
fragments.text: Use velocities immediately before and immediately after impact.

fragments.label: Momentum as a vector
fragments.text: Momentum: p=mv
Conservation equation

fragments.label: Conservation equation
fragments.text: For an isolated impact, total momentum before equals total momentum after. Include every body in the chosen system and keep the same positive direction on both sides.

fragments.label: Conservation equation
fragments.text: Internal impact forces cancel in the system total.

fragments.label: Conservation equation
fragments.text: External forces are neglected only over the short collision time.
Coalescing particles

fragments.label: Coalescing particles
fragments.text: If masses m₁ and m₂ stick together, their final mass is m₁+m₂ and they share velocity v: m₁u₁+m₂u₂=(m₁+m₂)v. The kinetic energy usually decreases, even though momentum is conserved.

fragments.label: Coalescing particles
fragments.text: Do not conserve kinetic energy unless justified.

fragments.label: Coalescing particles
fragments.text: Check whether v lies between the incoming signed velocities when appropriate.
Scope and interpretation

fragments.label: Scope and interpretation
fragments.text: This component examines one-dimensional direct impact and conservation. Impulse and coefficient of restitution are not required by the 2026–2027 Paper 4 syllabus. Focus on a clean before/after diagram and a signed momentum equation.

fragments.label: Scope and interpretation
fragments.text: Report direction with the final velocity.

fragments.label: Scope and interpretation
fragments.text: A body may reverse direction after impact.
Why are velocities signed in momentum work?

fragments.label: Why are velocities signed in momentum work?
fragments.text: Momentum is a vector, so direction must be represented.
What common velocity applies after coalescence?

fragments.label: What common velocity applies after coalescence?
fragments.text: Both bodies move with one velocity v and combined mass m₁+m₂.
Is kinetic energy always conserved in Paper 4 impacts?

fragments.label: Is kinetic energy always conserved in Paper 4 impacts?
fragments.text: No. Momentum is conserved for the isolated system; kinetic energy may be lost.
Are impulse and restitution required here?

fragments.label: Are impulse and restitution required here?
fragments.text: No; they are outside the stated 2026–2027 Mechanics content.

Apply F = ma to connected particles, pulleys and inclined planes. This guide turns the current syllabus outcomes into a connected revision sequence: learn the ideas, practise the method, then use the recall cards and checklist to diagnose what still needs work.

fragments.label: Resultant force
fragments.text: The vector sum of all external forces on a body.

fragments.label: Newton's second law
fragments.text: For constant mass, resultant force equals ma.

fragments.label: Tension
fragments.text: A pulling force transmitted by a taut string.

fragments.label: Light string
fragments.text: A string whose mass is neglected, allowing common tension in the ideal model.

fragments.label: Inextensible string
fragments.text: A string of fixed length, so connected particles share acceleration magnitude while taut.
Applying F=ma

fragments.label: Applying F=ma
fragments.text: Draw a force diagram for one body at a time, choose a positive direction, then write ΣF=ma in that direction. Forces opposite the positive direction enter negatively; acceleration uses the same sign convention.

fragments.label: Applying F=ma
fragments.text: F=ma uses resultant force, not any single force.

fragments.label: Applying F=ma
fragments.text: Equilibrium is the special case a=0.

fragments.label: Applying F=ma
fragments.text: Newton's second law: ΣF=ma
Vertical and inclined motion

fragments.label: Vertical and inclined motion
fragments.text: Resolve weight into mg sinθ along an incline and mg cosθ perpendicular. Friction opposes motion and can make upward and downward accelerations different. In vertical motion, weight remains downward throughout.

fragments.label: Vertical and inclined motion
fragments.text: Use R to determine friction where needed.

fragments.label: Vertical and inclined motion
fragments.text: At a turning point velocity is zero but the force and acceleration need not be.
Connected particles

fragments.label: Connected particles
fragments.text: For a light inextensible string over a smooth pulley, use one acceleration magnitude and common tension. Write a separate F=ma equation for each particle, then solve simultaneously. A whole-system equation can remove internal tension as a check.

fragments.label: Connected particles
fragments.text: Do not put forces from two different bodies on one free-body diagram.

fragments.label: Connected particles
fragments.text: Check that a computed tension is non-negative and the string remains taut.
Towing and thrust

fragments.label: Towing and thrust
fragments.text: A car and trailer have common acceleration while connected. Treat the tow-bar force as tension if pulling and thrust/compression if pushing. Use the whole system for acceleration, then one body for the connector force.

fragments.label: Towing and thrust
fragments.text: Resistance may act separately on each body.

fragments.label: Towing and thrust
fragments.text: Newton's third-law pair acts on different bodies.
What belongs on the left of F=ma?

fragments.label: What belongs on the left of F=ma?
fragments.text: The signed resultant of all forces on that one body.
Why do ideal connected particles share acceleration magnitude?

fragments.label: Why do ideal connected particles share acceleration magnitude?
fragments.text: The taut string is inextensible, so its length cannot change.
How can tension be eliminated?

fragments.label: How can tension be eliminated?
fragments.text: Apply F=ma to the whole connected system; tension is internal.
Can acceleration differ going up and down a rough incline?

fragments.label: Can acceleration differ going up and down a rough incline?
fragments.text: Yes, because friction reverses direction while gravity's component does not.

Calculate work done, kinetic/gravitational potential energy, and power in mechanical systems. This guide turns the current syllabus outcomes into a connected revision sequence: learn the ideas, practise the method, then use the recall cards and checklist to diagnose what still needs work.

fragments.label: Work
fragments.text: Energy transferred when a force acts through a displacement.

fragments.label: Kinetic energy
fragments.text: Energy associated with motion, ½mv².

fragments.label: Gravitational potential energy
fragments.text: Energy associated with height, mgh relative to a chosen datum.

fragments.label: Power
fragments.text: Rate of doing work or transferring energy.

fragments.label: Resistance
fragments.text: A force opposing motion and dissipating mechanical energy.
Work by a force

fragments.label: Work by a force
fragments.text: For constant force F and displacement d with angle θ between them, work is Fd cosθ. Work is positive when the force helps motion, negative when it opposes, and zero when perpendicular.

fragments.label: Work by a force
fragments.text: Use the angle between force and displacement, not automatically the slope angle.

fragments.label: Work by a force
fragments.text: Work has units joules.

fragments.label: Work by a force
fragments.text: Work: W=Fd cosθ
Energy stores

fragments.label: Energy stores
fragments.text: Kinetic energy is ½mv² and gravitational potential change is mgΔh. Only height change matters for GPE, even on a curved path. Choose a convenient zero level and use energy differences consistently.

fragments.label: Energy stores
fragments.text: Speed enters KE squared.

fragments.label: Energy stores
fragments.text: Mass cancels in some smooth gravity problems but not all.
Work–energy principle

fragments.label: Work–energy principle
fragments.text: Change in KE equals total work done by external forces. Equivalently, initial KE+GPE+work supplied equals final KE+GPE+energy dissipated. Include resistance as negative work or a positive loss, but not both.

fragments.label: Work–energy principle
fragments.text: Energy methods avoid time and often avoid resolving acceleration along a changing path.

fragments.label: Work–energy principle
fragments.text: Mechanical energy is conserved only when no non-conservative work is done.
Power

fragments.label: Power
fragments.text: Average power=work/time. Instantaneous power for a force parallel to motion is P=Fv. For a vehicle climbing at constant speed, driving power balances the rate of gain of GPE plus work against resistance.

fragments.label: Power
fragments.text: If acceleration is present, include ma in the force balance before using P=Fv.

fragments.label: Power
fragments.text: Convert kW to W.
When is work by a force zero?

fragments.label: When is work by a force zero?
fragments.text: When the force is perpendicular to the displacement.
What does change in kinetic energy equal?

fragments.label: What does change in kinetic energy equal?
fragments.text: The total work done by external forces.
Why does a curved smooth track still use mgh?

fragments.label: Why does a curved smooth track still use mgh?
fragments.text: Gravitational potential energy depends only on vertical height change.
When may P=Fv be used directly?

fragments.label: When may P=Fv be used directly?
fragments.text: For the force component acting in the direction of instantaneous motion.

Summarise and display data using histograms and cumulative frequency diagrams, and calculate mean, variance and standard deviation. This guide turns the current syllabus outcomes into a connected revision sequence: learn the ideas, practise the method, then use the recall cards and checklist to diagnose what still needs work.

fragments.label: Frequency density
fragments.text: Frequency divided by class width; histogram area represents frequency.

fragments.label: Interquartile range
fragments.text: Q₃−Q₁, the spread of the middle 50%.

fragments.label: Standard deviation
fragments.text: The square root of variance, measuring typical spread about the mean.

fragments.label: Cumulative frequency
fragments.text: A running total of observations up to a boundary.

fragments.label: Outlier
fragments.text: An observation unusually far from the rest; a common rule is below Q₁−1.5IQR or above Q₃+1.5IQR.
Choosing a display

fragments.label: Choosing a display
fragments.text: Stem-and-leaf retains raw values, box plots compare location/spread, cumulative frequency supports percentiles, and histograms show continuous grouped distributions. Discuss what information each preserves or hides.

fragments.label: Choosing a display
fragments.text: Use class boundaries for continuous data.

fragments.label: Choosing a display
fragments.text: A box width in a histogram is not a frequency by itself.

fragments.label: Choosing a display
fragments.text: Frequency density: frequency density=frequency/class width
Histograms

fragments.label: Histograms
fragments.text: For unequal class widths, vertical height is frequency density so bar area equals frequency. To recover frequency multiply density by class width. Label continuous boundaries and axes with units.

fragments.label: Histograms
fragments.text: Do not leave gaps between continuous classes.

fragments.label: Histograms
fragments.text: A changed vertical scale must still preserve area ratios.
Cumulative frequency

fragments.label: Cumulative frequency
fragments.text: Plot upper class boundaries against cumulative totals. Estimate Q₁, median and Q₃ at n/4, n/2 and 3n/4, reading horizontally to the curve then vertically to the value axis.

fragments.label: Cumulative frequency
fragments.text: Graph estimates should match the graph's precision.

fragments.label: Cumulative frequency
fragments.text: Percentile p uses pn/100.
Mean and variation

fragments.label: Mean and variation
fragments.text: Use x̄=Σx/n and variance=Σx²/n−x̄² for a population-style data set in this syllabus. For grouped data use class midpoints, so answers are estimates. Coding transforms totals and can simplify arithmetic.

fragments.label: Mean and variation
fragments.text: Compare both centre and spread in context.

fragments.label: Mean and variation
fragments.text: A smaller spread means greater consistency, not necessarily better performance.
What does histogram area represent?

fragments.label: What does histogram area represent?
fragments.text: Frequency, so height must be frequency density when class widths differ.
Where is the median read on a cumulative-frequency graph?

fragments.label: Where is the median read on a cumulative-frequency graph?
fragments.text: At cumulative frequency n/2.
Why are grouped-data statistics estimates?

fragments.label: Why are grouped-data statistics estimates?
fragments.text: Every value in a class is represented by its class midpoint.
What two features should a comparison mention?

fragments.label: What two features should a comparison mention?
fragments.text: A measure of location and a measure of spread, interpreted in context.

Count arrangements (order matters) and selections (order doesn't) using factorials, permutations and combinations. This guide turns the current syllabus outcomes into a connected revision sequence: learn the ideas, practise the method, then use the recall cards and checklist to diagnose what still needs work.

fragments.label: Permutation
fragments.text: An ordered arrangement.

fragments.label: Combination
fragments.text: An unordered selection.

fragments.label: Identical objects
fragments.text: Objects whose interchange creates no new arrangement.

fragments.label: Complementary counting
fragments.text: Counting all outcomes then subtracting forbidden outcomes.
Order versus selection

fragments.label: Order versus selection
fragments.text: Use ⁿPᵣ=n!/(n−r)! when order matters and ⁿCᵣ=n!/[r!(n−r)!] when it does not. Many problems combine a selection stage with a later arrangement stage; multiply the stage counts.

fragments.label: Order versus selection
fragments.text: Ask whether swapping two chosen objects changes the outcome.

fragments.label: Order versus selection
fragments.text: Explain each factor instead of presenting an unexplained product.

fragments.label: Order versus selection
fragments.text: Permutation: ⁿPᵣ=n!/(n−r)!
Repeated objects

fragments.label: Repeated objects
fragments.text: For n objects with repeated groups of sizes a,b,…, the number of distinct linear arrangements is n!/(a!b!…). Dividing removes permutations that look identical.

fragments.label: Repeated objects
fragments.text: Count the total number of letters carefully.

fragments.label: Repeated objects
fragments.text: Only divide for genuinely identical objects.
Objects together or apart

fragments.label: Objects together or apart
fragments.text: For objects that must stay together, treat the block as one object and multiply by internal orders. For 'not together', subtract together-cases from all arrangements. For separated identical objects, arrange the other objects and place them in gaps.

fragments.label: Objects together or apart
fragments.text: A block can appear in more than one internal order.

fragments.label: Objects together or apart
fragments.text: Gap methods need enough available gaps.
Position and grouping restrictions

fragments.label: Position and grouping restrictions
fragments.text: Handle fixed positions first, then arrange remaining objects. For rows or teams, select who occupies a group and then arrange within it if positions are distinct. Watch for double-counting when groups themselves are unlabelled.

fragments.label: Position and grouping restrictions
fragments.text: Circular arrangements are outside this syllabus.

fragments.label: Position and grouping restrictions
fragments.text: Cases should be mutually exclusive before adding.
When is ⁿCᵣ appropriate?

fragments.label: When is ⁿCᵣ appropriate?
fragments.text: When selecting r objects and the order of selection does not matter.
How do you count arrangements where A and B stay together?

fragments.label: How do you count arrangements where A and B stay together?
fragments.text: Treat AB as one block, arrange the blocks, then multiply by 2 for AB or BA.
How is 'A and B not together' often counted?

fragments.label: How is 'A and B not together' often counted?
fragments.text: All arrangements minus arrangements in which they form a block.
Why divide by a! for a identical objects?

fragments.label: Why divide by a! for a identical objects?
fragments.text: Their a! internal permutations produce no visibly different arrangement.

Use tree diagrams and Venn diagrams to handle conditional probability and test for independence. This guide turns the current syllabus outcomes into a connected revision sequence: learn the ideas, practise the method, then use the recall cards and checklist to diagnose what still needs work.

fragments.label: Mutually exclusive
fragments.text: Events that cannot occur together, so P(A∩B)=0.

fragments.label: Independent
fragments.text: Events where occurrence of one does not change the probability of the other.

fragments.label: Conditional probability
fragments.text: P(A|B), the probability of A given B has occurred.

fragments.label: Complement
fragments.text: A′, the event that A does not occur.

fragments.label: Sample space
fragments.text: The set of possible elementary outcomes.
Addition and multiplication

fragments.label: Addition and multiplication
fragments.text: For overlapping events, P(A∪B)=P(A)+P(B)−P(A∩B). Along successive branches multiply; across mutually exclusive complete routes add. Use complements for 'at least one'.

fragments.label: Addition and multiplication
fragments.text: Without replacement, branch probabilities change.

fragments.label: Addition and multiplication
fragments.text: Addition rule: P(A∪B)=P(A)+P(B)−P(A∩B)
Exclusive versus independent

fragments.label: Exclusive versus independent
fragments.text: Mutually exclusive non-zero events are not independent: if A occurs, B cannot. Test independence using P(A∩B)=P(A)P(B), or equivalently P(A|B)=P(A) when P(B)>0.

fragments.label: Exclusive versus independent
fragments.text: Do not infer independence from a diagram unless stated or shown.

fragments.label: Exclusive versus independent
fragments.text: Zero-probability edge cases need care.
Conditional probability

fragments.label: Conditional probability
fragments.text: Use P(A|B)=P(A∩B)/P(B). The denominator is the condition—the reduced sample space. Tree diagrams encode this because second-stage probabilities sit on branches after the condition is known.

fragments.label: Conditional probability
fragments.text: Read 'given that' before deciding the denominator.

fragments.label: Conditional probability
fragments.text: Reverse conditionals P(A|B) and P(B|A) are generally different.
Counting probability

fragments.label: Counting probability
fragments.text: When elementary outcomes are equally likely, probability=favourable/total. Use combinations for unordered selections and carefully account for colours, categories or restrictions in both numerator and denominator.

fragments.label: Counting probability
fragments.text: A Venn diagram can expose intersections and complements.

fragments.label: Counting probability
fragments.text: Check that final probabilities lie between 0 and 1.
Can two non-zero mutually exclusive events be independent?

fragments.label: Can two non-zero mutually exclusive events be independent?
fragments.text: No; occurrence of one makes the other impossible.
What is the denominator of P(A|B)?

fragments.label: What is the denominator of P(A|B)?
fragments.text: P(B), because B is the restricted sample space.
How is 'at least one' often simplified?

fragments.label: How is 'at least one' often simplified?
fragments.text: Use 1−P(none).
What changes in a without-replacement tree?

fragments.label: What changes in a without-replacement tree?
fragments.text: The second-stage totals and favourable counts depend on the first outcome.

Build probability distributions, calculate expectation and variance, and apply the binomial distribution. This guide turns the current syllabus outcomes into a connected revision sequence: learn the ideas, practise the method, then use the recall cards and checklist to diagnose what still needs work.

fragments.label: Discrete random variable
fragments.text: A variable taking separate countable numerical values.

fragments.label: Probability distribution
fragments.text: A table or rule assigning a probability to each possible value.

fragments.label: Expectation
fragments.text: The long-run mean E(X).

fragments.label: Binomial distribution
fragments.text: The number of successes in n independent fixed-probability trials.

fragments.label: Geometric distribution
fragments.text: The trial number of the first success in independent trials with probability p.
Distribution tables

fragments.label: Distribution tables
fragments.text: List every possible x and P(X=x), require each probability ≥0 and use ΣP(X=x)=1 to find constants. Then E(X)=ΣxP(X=x), E(X²)=Σx²P(X=x), and Var(X)=E(X²)−[E(X)]².

fragments.label: Distribution tables
fragments.text: Probabilities, not x-values, must sum to 1.

fragments.label: Distribution tables
fragments.text: Variance cannot be negative.

fragments.label: Distribution tables
fragments.text: Expectation: E(X)=ΣxP(X=x)
Binomial model

fragments.label: Binomial model
fragments.text: X~B(n,p) requires a fixed number n, two outcomes per trial, constant success probability p and independent trials. Use P(X=r)=ⁿCᵣpʳ(1−p)ⁿ⁻ʳ, with mean np and variance np(1−p).

fragments.label: Binomial model
fragments.text: Translate 'at most', 'fewer than' and 'at least' carefully.

fragments.label: Binomial model
fragments.text: Use complements for long upper tails.
Geometric model

fragments.label: Geometric model
fragments.text: For X~Geo(p), where X is the trial of first success, P(X=r)=p(1−p)ʳ⁻¹ and E(X)=1/p. The memoryless idea means after failures the chance of success on the next trial remains p.

fragments.label: Geometric model
fragments.text: The support begins at r=1, not 0.

fragments.label: Geometric model
fragments.text: Do not use a fixed n in a geometric model.
Using a calculator

fragments.label: Using a calculator
fragments.text: A calculator may evaluate cumulative probabilities, but the model, parameters and inequality conversion must be shown. For P(X>r), use 1−P(X≤r); for P(a≤X≤b), subtract cumulative values.

fragments.label: Using a calculator
fragments.text: Check whether calculator cumulative commands include the endpoint.

fragments.label: Using a calculator
fragments.text: State the distribution before the probability statement.
What four conditions support a binomial model?

fragments.label: What four conditions support a binomial model?
fragments.text: Fixed n, two outcomes, independent trials and constant success probability p.
What does a geometric variable count?

fragments.label: What does a geometric variable count?
fragments.text: The trial number on which the first success occurs.
How is Var(X) obtained from moments?

fragments.label: How is Var(X) obtained from moments?
fragments.text: E(X²)−[E(X)]².
How can P(X≥r) be written cumulatively?

fragments.label: How can P(X≥r) be written cumulatively?

fragments.text: Standardise normal variables to find probabilities, and use the inverse normal to find an unknown value or parameter. This guide turns the current syllabus outcomes into a connected revision sequence: learn the ideas, practise the method, then use the recall cards and checklist to diagnose what still needs work.

fragments.label: Normal distribution
fragments.text: A symmetric bell-shaped continuous distribution determined by mean μ and variance σ².

fragments.label: Standardisation
fragments.text: Converting X to Z=(X−μ)/σ with distribution N(0,1).

fragments.label: Continuity correction
fragments.text: Shifting a discrete boundary by 0.5 when using a continuous approximation.

fragments.label: Quantile
fragments.text: A value below which a stated proportion of the distribution lies.

fragments.label: Variance
fragments.text: σ²; the standard deviation is σ, not σ².
Normal model and sketches

fragments.label: Normal model and sketches
fragments.text: Write X~N(μ,σ²). The curve is symmetric about μ and total area is 1. Sketch and shade the required tail or interval before standardising; this catches complement and direction errors.

fragments.label: Normal model and sketches
fragments.text: A point probability is zero for a continuous variable.

fragments.label: Normal model and sketches
fragments.text: Use σ=√variance in z-scores.

fragments.label: Normal model and sketches
fragments.text: Standardisation: Z=(X−μ)/σ
Standardising

fragments.label: Standardising
fragments.text: For a boundary x, z=(x−μ)/σ. Use Φ(z)=P(Z≤z), symmetry Φ(−z)=1−Φ(z), and differences for intervals. Show the z-expression even when using a calculator directly.

fragments.label: Standardising
fragments.text: Retain full precision in z until the final probability.

fragments.label: Standardising
fragments.text: Standardise both endpoints separately.
Inverse normal questions

fragments.label: Inverse normal questions
fragments.text: Translate the stated area into a standard-normal quantile z, then solve x=μ+zσ. If μ or σ is unknown, each probability gives an equation. Use the sign of z based on whether the boundary lies below or above μ.

fragments.label: Inverse normal questions
fragments.text: A small lower-tail probability has negative z.

fragments.label: Inverse normal questions
fragments.text: Standard deviation must be positive.
Normal approximation to binomial

fragments.label: Normal approximation to binomial
fragments.text: For X~B(n,p), use Y~N(np,npq) when np>5 and nq>5, and apply continuity correction: X≤r becomes Y<r+0.5; X≥r becomes Y>r−0.5.

fragments.label: Normal approximation to binomial
fragments.text: Use q=1−p.

fragments.label: Normal approximation to binomial
fragments.text: Apply the correction before standardising.
What is the second parameter in N(μ,σ²)?

fragments.label: What is the second parameter in N(μ,σ²)?
fragments.text: The variance σ².
Which z corresponds to a boundary below μ?

fragments.label: Which z corresponds to a boundary below μ?
fragments.text: A negative z-score.
How is X≥12 continuity-corrected?

fragments.label: How is X≥12 continuity-corrected?
fragments.text: Use the continuous boundary Y>11.5.
When is the binomial normal approximation acceptable here?

fragments.label: When is the binomial normal approximation acceptable here?
fragments.text: When both np>5 and n(1−p)>5.

Model random events over a fixed time/space interval with the Poisson distribution, and know when it approximates the binomial. This guide turns the current syllabus outcomes into a connected revision sequence: learn the ideas, practise the method, then use the recall cards and checklist to diagnose what still needs work.

fragments.label: Poisson distribution
fragments.text: A count model for random events occurring independently at a constant average rate.

fragments.label: Parameter λ
fragments.text: The expected number of events in the stated interval; it is also the variance.

fragments.label: Rate
fragments.text: Expected events per unit time, length, area or volume.

fragments.label: Continuity correction
fragments.text: A ±0.5 boundary adjustment for a continuous normal approximation.

fragments.label: Rare event
fragments.text: An event with small probability per trial, supporting a Poisson approximation to binomial.
Poisson probabilities

fragments.label: Poisson probabilities
fragments.text: If X~Po(λ), then P(X=r)=e⁻ˡᵃᵐᵇᵈᵃ λʳ/r!, r=0,1,2,… . Mean and variance are λ. Use cumulative or complementary probabilities for ranges.

fragments.label: Poisson probabilities
fragments.text: The standard deviation is √λ.

fragments.label: Poisson probabilities
fragments.text: State the interval to which λ applies.

fragments.label: Poisson probabilities
fragments.text: Poisson mass: P(X=r)=e⁻λ λʳ/r!
Scaling the parameter

fragments.label: Scaling the parameter
fragments.text: A rate of c per unit gives λ=ct over t units, provided the rate is constant. Independent Poisson counts on disjoint intervals add, so parameters add too.

fragments.label: Scaling the parameter
fragments.text: Scale λ, not an observed count.

fragments.label: Scaling the parameter
fragments.text: Check that units match before multiplying.
Poisson approximation to binomial

fragments.label: Poisson approximation to binomial
fragments.text: For X~B(n,p), use Po(np) when n is large and p small; Cambridge gives approximately n>50 and np<5. The approximation removes the fixed upper bound, so use only when the tail beyond n is negligible.

fragments.label: Poisson approximation to binomial
fragments.text: Use λ=np.

fragments.label: Poisson approximation to binomial
fragments.text: No continuity correction is needed for Poisson-to-binomial because both are discrete.
Normal approximation to Poisson

fragments.label: Normal approximation to Poisson
fragments.text: When λ is large—approximately λ>15—use N(λ,λ) and apply a continuity correction. Standardise with standard deviation √λ.

fragments.label: Normal approximation to Poisson
fragments.text: Correct the integer boundary before finding z.

fragments.label: Normal approximation to Poisson
fragments.text: Sketch the tail to avoid complement errors.
What are the mean and variance of Po(λ)?

fragments.label: What are the mean and variance of Po(λ)?
fragments.text: Both equal λ.
How does λ change when an interval triples?

fragments.label: How does λ change when an interval triples?
fragments.text: It triples if the average rate stays constant.
When is Poisson a useful binomial approximation?

fragments.label: When is Poisson a useful binomial approximation?
fragments.text: For large n and small p, approximately n>50 and np<5 in this syllabus.
What normal model approximates Po(λ)?

fragments.label: What normal model approximates Po(λ)?
fragments.text: N(λ,λ), with a continuity correction, when λ is sufficiently large.

Find the expectation and variance of sums and differences of independent random variables. This guide turns the current syllabus outcomes into a connected revision sequence: learn the ideas, practise the method, then use the recall cards and checklist to diagnose what still needs work.

fragments.label: Linear combination
fragments.text: An expression such as aX+bY+c.

fragments.label: Independence
fragments.text: Knowledge of one variable gives no information about the other; required for adding variances here.

fragments.label: Covariance
fragments.text: A dependence measure; it is zero for independent variables, explaining the syllabus variance rule.

fragments.label: Affine transformation
fragments.text: A scaled-and-shifted variable aX+b.

fragments.label: Closure
fragments.text: A distribution family stays in the same family after a stated operation.
Expectation rules

fragments.label: Expectation rules
fragments.text: Expectation is linear whether or not variables are independent: E(aX+b)=aE(X)+b and E(aX+bY)=aE(X)+bE(Y). A constant shifts the mean directly.

fragments.label: Expectation rules
fragments.text: A negative coefficient subtracts the corresponding mean.

fragments.label: Expectation rules
fragments.text: Independence is not needed for expectation.

fragments.label: Expectation rules
fragments.text: Affine expectation: E(aX+b)=aE(X)+b
Variance rules

fragments.label: Variance rules
fragments.text: Var(aX+b)=a²Var(X); adding a constant changes no spread. For independent X,Y, Var(aX+bY)=a²Var(X)+b²Var(Y). The variances add even for X−Y because (−1)²=1.

fragments.label: Variance rules
fragments.text: Do not subtract variances for a difference.

fragments.label: Variance rules
fragments.text: Independence is essential for the syllabus formula.
Normal combinations

fragments.label: Normal combinations
fragments.text: If X and Y are independent normal variables, aX+bY is normal with mean aμₓ+bμᵧ and variance a²σₓ²+b²σᵧ². State the complete distribution before calculating a probability.

fragments.label: Normal combinations
fragments.text: Standard deviations do not add directly.

fragments.label: Normal combinations
fragments.text: A shift changes mean but not variance.
Poisson combinations

fragments.label: Poisson combinations
fragments.text: If independent X~Po(λ) and Y~Po(μ), then X+Y~Po(λ+μ). A difference is not Poisson. Splitting and combining counts requires independence and compatible intervals.

fragments.label: Poisson combinations
fragments.text: Only sums preserve the Poisson form here.

fragments.label: Poisson combinations
fragments.text: The parameters carry the same interval units.
Does independence matter for E(X+Y)?

fragments.label: Does independence matter for E(X+Y)?
fragments.text: No; expectation is linear regardless.
What is Var(X−Y) for independent X,Y?

fragments.label: What is Var(X−Y) for independent X,Y?
fragments.text: Var(X)+Var(Y).
What does adding a constant do to variance?

fragments.label: What does adding a constant do to variance?
fragments.text: Nothing; it shifts every value equally.
Is X−Y Poisson when X and Y are Poisson?

fragments.label: Is X−Y Poisson when X and Y are Poisson?
fragments.text: No. Only the independent sum has the stated Poisson closure property.

Use probability density functions and integration to find probabilities, expectation and variance for continuous variables. This guide turns the current syllabus outcomes into a connected revision sequence: learn the ideas, practise the method, then use the recall cards and checklist to diagnose what still needs work.

fragments.label: Continuous random variable
fragments.text: A variable able to take any real value in an interval.

fragments.label: Probability density function
fragments.text: A non-negative function whose area over an interval gives probability and whose total area is 1.

fragments.label: Density
fragments.text: Height per unit x; it can exceed 1 provided areas are valid probabilities.

fragments.label: Median
fragments.text: A value m with equal probability on either side for a continuous distribution.

fragments.label: Support
fragments.text: The interval on which the density is non-zero.
Valid density functions

fragments.label: Valid density functions
fragments.text: A pdf f(x) must satisfy f(x)≥0 on its support and ∫f(x)dx=1 over the whole support. Use normalisation to find unknown constants, checking they keep the density non-negative.

fragments.label: Valid density functions
fragments.text: A density value is not itself a point probability.

fragments.label: Valid density functions
fragments.text: Outside the stated support, f(x)=0.

fragments.label: Valid density functions
fragments.text: Normalisation: ∫ f(x) dx=1 over the support
Probabilities as areas

fragments.label: Probabilities as areas
fragments.text: P(a < X < b)=∫ₐᵇf(x)dx after intersecting the requested interval with the support. For continuous X, endpoints make no difference: P(X=a)=0.

fragments.label: Probabilities as areas
fragments.text: Draw the support and shade the required interval.

fragments.label: Probabilities as areas
fragments.text: Use complements for awkward tails.
Percentiles

fragments.label: Percentiles
fragments.text: A pth percentile q satisfies ∫ from the lower support limit to q of f(x)dx=p/100. The median uses 0.5. Solve and select the root that lies within the support.

fragments.label: Percentiles
fragments.text: Do not assume median equals mean unless symmetry justifies it.

fragments.label: Percentiles
